June Bernstein

June Bernstein   Director of public information at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, dean of students at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, and co-editor of this journal. She is a faculty member, training analyst, and supervisor at both institutes and practices in New York City and Boston.

How do we get our patients and students to relinquish their self-destructive, self-critical modes of operating? In attempting to answer this question, the author examines ways in which criticism is both expressed and experienced in the consulting room and in the classroom. Numerous case examples provide insight into the dynamics associated with giving and receiving criticism.

Psychoanalysts, who have seen their own work mischaracterized as insulated within a hermetic subculture of fanciful notions, might balk at a comparison between psychoanalysis and Romanticism. This paper discusses how some of the reflecting techniques of modern analysis and the tendency to avoid anything ego-oriented may keep analysts and patients locked into the status quo phase of analysis. The fear of losing the patient may motivate some therapists to be so careful that patients are not helped to recognize and move beyond their repetitions. In order to reach the stages of progressive communication and cooperation, patients must be given the chance to know themselves through ego-syntonic explanations and to consciously decide to work with the analyst.

The problem around the exchange of money in therapeutic relationships has many dimensions and can be viewed- or justified—from different theoretical or even ideological perspectives. The intrusion of the analyst's need into the therapeutic relation is often the culprit. Using Jacques-Alain Miller's language, the author argues that when it comes to matters of money, the analyst's unconscious at times reveals itself in a bizarre manner. This is particularly true when the analyst pockets the change if a naïve patient gives him a large bill. The reasoning is that the patient's unconscious has interpreted—fixed—a new price for his or her analysis. The question is: Would the analyst reduce the fee if the patient “unconsciously” gave him or her a small bill, i.e., less than the

*“Did You Say Bizarre?” is the title of a 1999 presentation by Jacques-Alain Miller at New York University. Miller contends that the analytic session is a monologue except when the analyst makes an interpretation, which Miller thinks is, in itself, always a bizarre mode of speech. He also maintains that the unconscious always reveals itself in a bizarre manner. The implication is evidently Miller's understanding of Jacques Lacan's conduct in analytic sessions. For Lacanians, another explanation of this behavior is to argue that Lacan intentionally tried to exhibit—enact—the language of the unconscious.189

stipulated fee? If the analyst listens to the patient's unconscious by increasing the fee in the former case, why not equally listen to the unconscious by reducing the fee in the latter case? Should the analyst listen to the patient's unconscious only when it is in his or her self-interest? In such instances, it is more plausible to contend that the analyst listens to the unconscious language of capitalism.

Emotional Communication: Countertransference Analysis and the Use of Feeling in Psychoanalytic Technique. Paul Geltner. New York: Routledge, 2013. 336 pp.

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall  

Paul Geltner has authored a book that will interest students and practitioners of psychoanalysis; novices will also be attracted to his system, his “experience near” language, and extensive clinical dialogues; modern psychoanalysts will feel refreshed and empowered by his reasoned perspective; supervisors will embrace his flexible systematic approach to common, stubborn clinical impasses; theoreticians will be intrigued by his attempt to provide a system that evolves hypotheses for clinical testing; and all clinicians will appreciate and want to further study his practical approach to everyday thorny issues.

I first read Geltner's book by browsing the whole in an emotional mode. I then reread and studied it in a more comprehensive, cognitive manner. This approach is suggested because in the first half Geltner outlines the theoretical structure of his theory, which is needed to appreciate the logic and artistry of the lively clinical techniques illustrated in the second half.

Geltner constructs a conceptual synthesis of a minority tradition in psychoanalysis. The minority tradition includes many modern psychoanalysts, especially Spotnitz. In fact, Geltner's book could readily be subtitled A Theory of Technique, the same subtitle as Spotnitz's (2004) seminal publication, Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic Patient.

Wasting Time in Analysis: The Lure of Repetition

June Bernstein PHD

June Bernstein

16 Gerlach Place
Larchmont, NY 10538
junstein@verizon.net

June Bernstein   Director of public information at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, dean of students at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, and co-editor of this journal. She is a faculty member, training analyst, and supervisor at both institutes and practices in New York City and Boston.

Why does analysis take so long? Destructive urges associated with the death instinct and the repetition compulsion give a conceptual framework for the existence of time-wasting in analysis. Constructive ends may also be served by repetition. Repetition may offer pleasure, mastery, and the conservation of needed relationships, including the maintenance of a long-term relationship with the analyst. Modern analysis has developed some specific theories and techniques which have relevance to this issue. The analytic relationship is an example of a favorable outcome of the ability to spend a lot of time before mutative change takes place.

He also is a faculty member and supervisor at the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Study Center, and Westchester Institute for Training in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy, and a member of the Lacanian Clinical Forum and ISPS. A philosophical and psychoanalytic memoir, this paper attempts to show, rather than argue, how the author's thinking has evolved over 50 years of engagement with philosophy and psychoanalysis. The effect of this reflection is to reveal some of the most basic features of thinking and of the unfolding of a psychoanalytic dialogue. The various philosophical and psychoanalytic approaches considered are treated as evolving discourses originating in the Other. The author gradually has assumed them, or at least features of them, as his own. At the end he is in position to say something, and indeed, to have something to say. Finally, he makes the argument that such an outcome is the goal of psychoanalysis, constituting its logical end.

Eugene Goldwater   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who practices in Hadley and Brookline, MA and teaches at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. He has taught, lectured, and written about numerous subjects, including fantasy and creativity, childhood and maturation, men and women, sex and violence, and happiness and the principle of “good enough.”

Mysterious phenomena such as symbolic communications and unexpected transformations have sometimes been attributed to supernatural influences, i.e., magic, in our daily lives. Psychoanalysis understands these experiences as the manifestations of unconscious mental processes. The study of magic in life and in literature provides another way of accessing these processes. The relationship between magical thinking and rational thinking was central to two of the most influential books of the twentieth century: “The Interpretation of Dreams” by Sigmund Freud (1900/1953) and The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900). Coming from completely different intellectual domains, these two works presented strikingly similar approaches to the problem of how to integrate conscious and unconscious experience in the interests of survival in the real world. This paper demonstrates the existence of apparent magical influences in everyday life, describes Baum's modern theory of magic, and further illustrates the overlap between psychoanalysis and magic by giving some examples of psychoanalytic spells.

Catch Them Before They Fall: The Psychoanalysis of Breakdown. Christopher Bollas. New York: Taylor & Francis, 2013. 152 pp.

Tracy Morgan

Tracy Morgan

Tracy Morgan  

Having spent nearly forty years as a “practitioner of the unconscious” (P. Gherovici, personal communication, May, 2012), Christopher Bollas is arguably one of the most creative minds at work in the English-speaking psychoanalytic world. Though he is a more controversial figure in England where his critique of things Kleinian is not so welcome, his more than 13 books

299

and countless journal articles are taught at a myriad of North American psychoanalytic institutes. Given the diversity and contentiousness among schools of thought, this is no small feat.

That he has developed his own metapsychology, one that reflects his encounters with analysts and analytic thinking that range from Bion to Coltart, from Freeman-Sharpe to Lacan, and from Khan to Phillips, not to mention Winnicott, is both significant and breathtaking. While he has not yet been fully acknowledged for this accomplishment, allow yourself to ponder the following terms that since the late 1980s he has generated and elaborated (in doing so, you may have an “aha” moment): the “receptive unconscious,” the “un-thought known,” the “human idiom,” and “psychic genera,” to name just a few. They knit themselves together to form a particular view of human experience at the level of the psyche: the weave is tight.

In Catch Them Before They Fall: The Psychoanalysis of Breakdown, Bollas's metapsychology comes to life, although much of it is implied, providing the vital roots for his clinical decision-making. Having for many years quite surreptitiously attended to patients on the cusp of psychic disarray primarily by using the talking cure (aka psychoanalysis), albeit altering the frame of its practice as needed, he makes a powerful argument that can be heard as a wake-up call for the profession as well as a clinical primer on working with psychic breakdown.

In what can be read as a kind of political declaration, Bollas writes the following: “Psychoanalysis is the treatment of choice [italics added] for patients who are breaking down” (p. 7). If this is not the laying down of a gauntlet regarding the treatment in 2013 of a mental breakdown, what is it? When encountered on the page, this plainspoken statement practically vivisects. Why is this so? Recall that the DSM once freely employed psychoanalytic concepts in defining its diagnoses, and you will sense how far we/you/I may have drifted.

Loryn Hatch   Received her master's degree at the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis in 2012. She is currently a PhD student in clinical psychology at City College in New York. She lives in Brooklyn.

For the psychoanalytic mind, the ubiquitous phrase “I don't know” resonates with unconscious power. The phrase implies that, in fact, there is something to be known. This paper looks at the recurring appearance of “I don't know” in excerpts from one and a half years of sessions with a middle aged man, “G,” observed during a psychoanalytic externship through the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. Using the concepts of “symbolization,” the making of meaning through symbols, and “desymbolization,” the destruction of meaning through defenses such as denial, disavowal, and going blank, the evolution in meaning and function of “I don't know” for G is studied. This paper suggests that through the influence of a symbolizing, analytic perspective, the initial desymbolized state of G transforms to a more reflective, symbolized state.

responseSet.title: Introduction
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Introduction

June Bernstein's gaze directed at modern psychoanalytic thinking, writing, and teaching has been penetrating and her reflections on and reconsiderations of some of the central concepts of our theory of technique have been clarifying. And so, equally, have been her open-minded, evenhanded reports on the thinking of other contemporary practitioners and theorists who have paid particular attention to the narcissistic disorders.

The papers draw on a wide range of modern and classical ideas. “There's No Such Thing As a Mother” describes Meadow's drive theory, which focuses on the patient's unconscious rather than on the influence of the mother. “Psychic Truth and the Bible” takes note of the parallels between the account of creation found in Genesis and an infant's developmental sequences, and finds that the wish to be worshipped to the exclusion of all others motivates man as well as God. “Magic in the Analysis” demonstrates the sometimes uncanny effect of analytic work.

Other papers focus on the use of modern analytic techniques and their theoretical underpinnings. These include “An Approach to the Management of Treatment Impasses,” which illustrates the use of emotional communication; “Current Trends in the Treatment Of Narcissism,” which succinctly compares the theories and techniques of Kohut, Kernberg, and Spotnitz; and “Using the Countertransference Resistance,” which demonstrates how the therapist's subjective countertransference can lead to productive investigation.

Aggressive wishes may motivate impulsivity and inhibition. Since destructive impulsivity seems most likely to occur when the patient has no commitments to anyone, modern psychoanalysts focus first on fostering a narcissistic transference within which a patient may discharge tension in the presence of another person. When the repetition compulsion enters the transference, the patient is driven to repeat negative emotional experiences with the analyst. This resistance to progress is viewed as a special form of impulse disorder. Commands, prohibitions, and emotional communications are used to enable the patient to have new emotional experiences in the transference.

A Resistance to Getting Better

June Bernstein PHD

June Bernstein

16 Gerlach Place

junstein@verizon.net

June Bernstein   Director of public information at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, dean of students at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, and co-editor of this journal. She is a faculty member, training analyst, and supervisor at both institutes and practices in New York City and Boston.

This paper considers the ways in which getting even, at times a healthy response, may, if it becomes the major motivational force in life, interfere with maturation and getting better.
